Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-09-16 16:00 PT
- Duration: 52 minutes
- Attendees: Lena Morales (Redwood AE), Connor Zhang (Redwood SE), Maya Rao (Auriga CTO), Erik Lund (Platform Lead), Priya Shah (Eng Manager), Samir Patel (Procurement)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be rough):
Auriga is evaluating hosting options (hosted vs dedicated vs private) primarily on unit economics and predictable monthly cost. Key constraints: 200 QPS average peak, 150ms latency SLO for customer-facing paths, monthly budget ~USD 100k-150k for inference. Discussed batching, KV-prefix caching, quantization tradeoffs, and reserved capacity vs pay-as-you-go. Action items: Redwood to deliver tailored pricing scenarios and run a simulation; customer to share exact token volumes and security expectations.

Topics:
- Cost per token & billing model comparisons
- Batching/caching/quantization levers to reduce per-token cost
- Tradeoffs between Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (predictability, data control)
- Security/compliance (SOC 2, KMS, SSO)

Transcript body (timestamps approximate, transcription may contain errors):
00:00 Lena Morales: All right hi everyone thanks for joining, uh, we're gonna kick off, I'm Lena from Redwood, Connor's with me, we'll run through cost levers and then dive into some specifics for Auriga, thanks for the intros.
00:10 Maya Rao: Hey thanks, we've got a couple engineers and procurement on the line. Quick note we're evaluating both a hosted option and reserved capacity, also exploring on-prem later. Main thing is unit economics and predictable monthly spend.
00:22 Connor Zhang: Great. To start can you give rough traffic shape? QPS, burst patterns, average token lengths?
00:28 Erik Lund: Yeah we're seeing roughly 150 to 220 QPS during peak for the chat endpoint, average prompt+completion around 450 tokens, but there's a long tail where analytic jobs hit 3-4k tokens.
00:40 Priya Shah: Also, a big chunk is short assistant messages — like 40-70 tokens — but the billing math is messy when mixed.
00:47 Lena Morales: Right, that mix matters a ton for batching efficiency and whether prefix cache helps. Quick question on SLOs, Maya? You mentioned 150ms — is that 95th or p95?
00:57 Maya Rao: p95 yes, for user-facing flows. Background analytic jobs can be slower. We can cap background batch windows to a minute or two.
01:06 Connor Zhang: Okay good. High-level levers we typically recommend: 1) model size/variant selection (cheaper smaller models for non-critical flows), 2) batching and continuous batching to increase GPU utilization, 3) KV/prefix caching for repeated prompts, 4) quantization and int8/4-bit strategies, and 5) reserved/dedicated pools for predictable unit cost.
01:28 Samir Patel: From procurement we care about predictability. Hosted variable billing is scary for budget planning. What does Redwood offer for smoothing cost?
01:36 Lena Morales: We do usage-based for hosted, plus Reserved (Dedicated) capacity where you commit to capacity and get lower per-token equivalent. Dedicated gives you stable throughput and a monthly commit. For private on-prem there's a different commercial model — more like license + infra run cost.
01:50 Erik Lund: Can you share example math? Like if we commit to a pool for 200 QPS, what does that cost vs pay-as-you-go?
01:57 Connor Zhang: Sure, rough example, using our public ranges: for a general-purpose open model at 1.5B-ish equivalent, pay-as-you-go token cost might be X cents per 1k tokens, whereas a dedicated pool amortized with utilization and batching can drop effective cost by 30-60% depending on batch depth and cache hit rate. I don't want to throw exact numbers without your exact token mix, but we can model.
02:20 Maya Rao: We have a rough monthly token estimate — around 1.5B tokens across endpoints, with 65% user messages and 35% background. Does that tilt you toward dedicated?
02:29 Connor Zhang: For 1.5B tokens/month with a steady 200 QPS peak, Dedicated often makes sense for predictable cost, especially if you can hit moderate batching gains and caching. But two caveats: if your traffic is extremely spiky and mostly short tokens, hosted with autoscaling can be cheaper short term.
02:44 Priya Shah: About caching — our product has a lot of repeated prefixes for similar prompts. How much does a prefix/KV cache reduce tokens?
02:51 Connor Zhang: If you have strong repetition, prefix caching can reduce model compute by 30-70% for certain flows. We saw a customer with conversational fallbacks cut per-request decode tokens by 45% on average. But it requires controlling prompt formats and integration to reuse context effectively.
03:10 Maya Rao: And batching — our UX needs sub-200ms p95, will batching push latency above that?
03:16 Connor Zhang: Continuous batching techniques can keep small-request latency low: we use micro-batching windows that are adaptive — you can set max wait times (e.g., 10ms-40ms) to balance latency vs token-per-GPU gains. For a p95 of 150ms it's feasible, but we need to test with your exact traffic.
03:32 Samir Patel: Security question — if we go Dedicated or Private, how does KMS work? We have a requirement to manage keys in our HSM for certain PII flows.
03:40 Lena Morales: For Dedicated and Private we support customer-managed KMS/HSM integrations. Private gives you full control of keys. Dedicated integrates with our key wrap model where you can bring your own keys via a supported KMS. We'll include the KMS integration notes in the checklist.
03:52 Erik Lund: Do you have SOC 2 and logs for auditing? We need full audit trails for compliance.
03:57 Lena Morales: Yes SOC 2 Type II, and we provide audit logs with per-request metadata, token counts, and per-route latency. For Private you can keep logs on-prem or send to your SIEM.
04:07 Maya Rao: Great. On model variants, could we run smaller model for quick answers and fallback to a larger one for complex queries? How does billing work?
04:16 Connor Zhang: Absolutely — multi-tier routing is a common pattern. Routing policies let you send low-critical traffic to small models and only escalate when quality checks fail. Billing is per-request per-model compute; our platform can show token and cost attribution per route so you can see the blended unit economics.
04:30 Priya Shah: One concern: if we use hosted for a bit and then move to Private later, how hard is migration? We want minimal app-level changes.
04:37 Lena Morales: We designed the API to be consistent across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private. The migration is mainly infra and auth config. You can pin model versions and rollout policies so application code stays stable.
04:46 Erik Lund: Ok, let's talk numbers. We can handle a $120k/mo inference budget if it covers all interactive and background workloads. Can Redwood model scenarios where background batch windows are 60s and interactive p95 is 150ms?
04:58 Connor Zhang: Yes, we'll run three scenarios: 1) Hosted with autoscale and median batching, 2) Dedicated reserved pool sized for 200 QPS with moderate batching/caching, 3) Private with an infra cost estimate and license. We'll include token-level breakouts and expected unit cost.
05:14 Maya Rao: Any quick wins on cost we should try now?
05:18 Connor Zhang: Start by identifying high-repeat prefixes and instrumenting caching. Also route non-critical loads to smaller models and implement simple response length caps for certain endpoints. Quantization is also a high-impact lever especially for CPU or low-cost GPU stacks.
05:30 Priya Shah: Regarding quantization, do you do quantization-aware kernels or is it just model file transforms? We're concerned about quality delta.
05:36 Connor Zhang: We use runtime kernels optimized for int8/4-bit execution that preserve quality for many transformer architectures. We'll share our evals; some tasks see minimal quality drop, others less so. It's workload dependent.
05:48 Erik Lund: When you talk about 30-60% savings, is that after including increased developer time and integration work?
05:54 Lena Morales: The numbers are purely execution cost comparisons. We'll include estimated integration effort as a separate line item — typically a few engineer-weeks to implement caching and routing, less if you already have instrumentation. We'll call that out explicitly.
06:10 Samir Patel: Procurement timeline — we probably need a PO in ~6 weeks if the numbers work, otherwise delayed to next quarter. Any deal incentives for committed annual contracts?
06:20 Lena Morales: Yes we have committed contracts with discounts for annual reserved capacity. We'll provide a pricing sheet with tiered discounts.
06:27 Maya Rao: Questions from my side on fallback behaviors — if a model saturates, can Redwood automatically fall back to a cheaper/approx model to preserve throughput?
06:35 Connor Zhang: Yes, routing policies support automated fallbacks by model family or region. You can set cost-first or latency-first fallbacks. We'll show examples in the scenario doc.
06:45 Maya Rao: Cool. A random note: some model names in the public docs are garbled in transcripts, but we can ignore that.
06:50 Lena Morales: lol, yeah auto-transcripts scramble names sometimes.
06:54 (background murmur)
07:10 Priya Shah: On observability: can we see token-level attribution by customer route and by model? We want to allocate costs per product team.
07:18 Connor Zhang: Yes, Console gives token and cost attribution by tag/route, plus traces. You can invoice internal teams based on per-route usage.
07:26 Erik Lund: Any caveats on multi-tenancy if we choose dedicated? We need strict isolation for some customers.
07:33 Lena Morales: Dedicated provides capacity isolation; for strict tenancy you can opt for private on-prem or VPC private deployment. We'll map the isolation guarantees in the checklist.
07:42 Maya Rao: This is great. Can Connor also simulate worst-case burst — say 500 QPS for two minutes — to see latency degradation vs cost?
07:50 Connor Zhang: Yes we'll simulate bursts and show tail latency and fallback costs. Expect heavier tails to push you toward higher reserved headroom or cross-region fallback.
07:59 Samir Patel: Anything else procurement needs to know about invoicing and data residency?
08:05 Lena Morales: We support invoicing on monthly billing for enterprise, and we have region controls for data residency. We'll include commercial terms for review.
